title: Actuators
summary: Contactors and motors, solenoid valves, pumps and lamps: what the PLC switches and what feedback it gets back.
objectives: Use feedback to confirm an actuator moved

sections.heading: Doing work
sections.body: A PLC output rarely drives a motor directly. It energizes a **contactor coil**, which switches the motor power. A **solenoid valve** opens with 24 V. **Pumps** and **fans** are motors. Lamps and horns signal to people.

sections.heading: Command and feedback
sections.body: Good designs check that a command really had an effect.
sections.diagram:
PLC DO --> contactor coil K1 --> motor M1
  PLC DI <-- K1 auxiliary contact (feedback)
  PLC DI <-- valve limit switch (open / closed)

sections.heading: Feedback check
sections.body: Detect a contactor that did not pull in.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: Assuming an actuator moved because the output is TRUE. Valves stick, fuses blow and contactors fail. Without feedback the program cannot know.

question.question: The output is TRUE and its LED is on, but the valve stays closed. Where is the fault?
options: Between the output terminal and the valve
question.explanation: The PLC did its part; the field side did not respond.

sections.heading: Watch command and response
sections.body: On the tank station, watch the valve command, the valve position and the flow.

sections.heading: Summary and troubleshooting note
sections.body:
Outputs command actuators through contactors and solenoids; feedback signals confirm they responded.

**Troubleshooting note:** If an output is TRUE but nothing moves, check the module's load supply, the fuse, the wiring and the actuator itself.

checkpoint.question: What switches the power of a large motor?
checkpoint.explanation: The PLC output drives the contactor coil.

checkpoint.question: Why use a valve limit switch?
options: To confirm the valve really moved
